lines.text: A replica is supposed to end up with everything its primary has.
That word, everything, is doing a lot of work. It can mean two genuinely different things to actually send across the wire.
Both of them get called replication. Only one of them is replicating the same bytes.
The first answer is the exact one. Send the actual blocks, byte for byte, address for address.
It's fast and cheap to apply, because the replica never has to figure anything out. It just writes the same bytes in the same place.
The cost of that simplicity is strictness. Both sides have to be running the identical version of the database engine.
The second answer throws away the bytes entirely and sends something higher level instead.
Decode the write-ahead log back into the actual row that changed, and send that instead of raw storage.
Now the two sides don't have to match at all. Different versions, even different operating systems, can read the same decoded change.
Here's where I want you to actually commit to an answer.
Picture a consumer on the other end of one of these streams that simply stops reading. What happens to all the data it hasn't picked up yet?
It's tempting to assume the primary eventually just cleans up and moves on.
But the primary has no way to know whether that consumer is gone for good or just slow. Guessing wrong either way is dangerous.
So it doesn't guess. It keeps every bit the consumer hasn't confirmed, for however long that takes.
That keeping is a real, named mechanism, not an accident.
A replication slot is the primary's own promise to a specific consumer. Don't you dare remove anything I might still need.
The primary holds up its end of that promise completely, with no built in sense of how long is too long.
Here's that exact promise, held for real, against this sandbox's own database.
A real slot gets created, and then real writes just keep landing, with absolutely nothing on the other end ever reading them.
Watch what the primary ends up holding onto on that one consumer's behalf. It just keeps growing.
